query: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, and how is it defined?

plan.title: Defining the Speed of Light
plan_steps: This research will identify the precise numerical value of the speed of light in a vacuum as established by international standards.
It will further investigate the historical shift in the SI system that redefined the meter based on this constant.
search_queries: exact speed of light in vacuum m/s
how is the speed of light defined in SI units
history of the definition of the meter and speed of light
is the speed of light a defined constant or measured value

answer.raw_answer:
## Summary
The speed of light in a vacuum, denoted by the constant $c$, is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. This value is not a measurement but a fixed definition established by international agreement, which in turn defines the length of the meter.

## The Numerical Value and Definition of $c$
The speed of light in a vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 meters per second [The Speed of Light: What Is c and Why Is It Constant? — physicsfundamentals.org](https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/speed-of-light). This constant, $c$, represents the speed at which all electromagnetic radiation—including radio waves, visible light, and X-rays—travels through a vacuum [The Speed of Light: What Is c and Why Is It Constant? — physicsfundamentals.org](https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/speed-of-light).

<details>
<summary>Historical context and the definition of the meter</summary>

The current definition of the meter is derived directly from the speed of light. Specifically, one meter is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second [The Speed of Light: What Is c and Why Is It Constant? — physicsfundamentals.org](https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/speed-of-light). 

This definition was adopted to link the unit of length to an invariant of nature, moving away from reliance on physical artifacts [Resolution 1 of the 24th CGPM (2011) - BIPM — www.bipm.org](https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/24-2011/resolution-1). The specific value of 299,792,458 m/s was chosen because it was the established value of the speed of light at the time of the 1983 definition, with an uncertainty of approximately ±1 m/s; adopting this specific number ensured continuity with previous measurements rather than rounding to a "cleaner" number like 300,000,000 m/s [history - Why wasn't the meter defined using a round-number fraction (like 1/300 000 000) of the distance travelled by light in 1 second? - Physics Stack Exchange — physics.stackexchange.com](https://physics.stackexchange.com/questions/112096/why-wasnt-the-meter-defined-using-a-round-number-fraction-like-1-300-000-000).
</details>

## Speed of Light in Different Media
While the speed of light in a vacuum is a universal constant, light travels more slowly when passing through various materials. The speed in a medium is determined by the refractive index ($n$) of that material, calculated as $v = c/n$ [The Speed of Light: What Is c and Why Is It Constant? — physicsfundamentals.org](https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/speed-of-light).

| Medium | Refractive Index ($n$) | Speed of Light (approx.) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Vacuum | 1.000 (exact) | 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s |
| Air | 1.0003 | 2.997 × 10⁸ m/s |
| Water | 1.33 | 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s |
| Crown glass | 1.52 | 1.97 × 10⁸ m/s |
| Diamond | 2.42 | 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s |

<details>
<summary>Additional context on light speed in media</summary>

When particles travel through a medium faster than the speed of light in that specific medium (though still slower than $c$ in a vacuum), they emit Cherenkov radiation. This phenomenon manifests as a blue electromagnetic shock wave, similar to a sonic boom, and is the reason nuclear reactor cores often appear to glow blue when submerged in water [The Speed of Light: What Is c and Why Is It Constant? — physicsfundamentals.org](https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/speed-of-light).
</details>

## Key Takeaways
*   **Exact Value:** The speed of light in a vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 m/s.
*   **Definition:** The meter is defined by this constant; it is the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
*   **Universality:** $c$ is the speed limit of the universe, applying to all electromagnetic radiation and massless particles.
*   **Media Impact:** Light slows down in materials based on their refractive index, which can lead to phenomena like Cherenkov radiation.
